A coding agent that meets 70% of your requirements has not finished 70% of your work.

Co-Design Bench, a new benchmark from Alibaba and university researchers (arXiv, October 26), built 273 revision tasks from 26,314 real user coding sessions. Each task is an existing web app plus a user's request, sometimes with an image, video, audio clip or document. Agents are graded against 2,331 hidden acceptance criteria, and a separate verifier challenges every pass for stubs, hardcoding and unreachable features.

Results for ten models in one shared harness:

1. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, passed 69.9% of criteria per task on average but fully delivered only 26.4% of tasks. Opus 5 was next at 18.3%.
2. Scope hurts. On localized edits, GPT-6 Astra fully delivered 41.0% of tasks. On coordinated changes across a multi-file repo, 17.9%.
3. Breadth hurts every model. All ten scored lower on repo edits that needed three or four kinds of change than on edits needing one or two.
4. Effort is not completion. On localized edits, GLM-5.2 used 69 turns and 7.29M tokens per task for 57.2% of criteria passed. GPT-6 Astra used 32 turns and 1.24M tokens for 75.4%.

Partial credit hides where the work was left. The one criterion an agent missed may be the first thing a user notices, so a "mostly done" run still needs someone to find the gap.

For builders, that argues for three habits: write acceptance criteria before the agent starts, check each one after, and split broad requests into narrow ones.

Caveat: tasks were ranked partly by difficulty and past failure signals, so 26.4% is not an everyday success rate.

$PAGS Q3 2026 earnings: PagBank's banking profit grows fast, but its payment revenue shrinks

PagBank's banking division and lower funding costs lifted third-quarter profit even as its core payment-processing business shrank. Gross profit rose 4% from a year ago to R$2.0 billion, while profit per share excluding one-offs climbed 13% to R$2.19 with help from share buybacks. Chief executive Carlos Mauad highlighted a 73% jump in working capital and credit card loans, which pushed the total credit book up 25% to R$5.2 billion.

• Revenue, excluding card fees: 𝐑$𝟑,𝟒𝟐𝟒𝐌 (+0.4% from a year ago)
• Gross profit: 𝐑$𝟐,𝟎𝟎𝟎𝐌 (+3.8% from a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: 𝐑$𝟐.𝟏𝟗 (+13.2% from a year ago)
• Capital return outlook: 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐝 (~R$400M dividend in Dec; >=R$2B to 2028)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because faster unsecured lending and lower deposit costs offset a steeper drop in merchant payment prepayments. Expanding into higher-yield working capital loans lifted banking gross profit by 18%, and lower Brazilian interest rates cut funding expenses by 7%. One caution: shifting toward unsecured credit pushed the 90-day loan default rate up to 3.8% from 2.6% a year ago, more than doubling quarterly loan loss provisions.

The question now is whether small business lending can keep growing without credit defaults eating up the extra interest income. If underwriting holds up, higher banking margins will carry earnings; if defaults keep rising as recent loan cohorts age, provisions will stall profit growth. Fourth-quarter delinquency rates and loan loss provisions will show which way the book is trending.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
PagBank, a Brazilian digital bank and payment processor for small businesses and consumers, relies on its banking division to offset a slow card-processing business. Chief executive Carlos Mauad wants loans and digital accounts to deepen customer relationships and lift revenue per client.

That banking division carried the third quarter. "Our Working Capital and Credit Card portfolios combined grew 73% year-over-year, driven by a particularly strong acceleration in Working Capital origination during the quarter," Mauad wrote. The company issued R$299 million in new working capital loans to merchants, with lending picking up pace in September.

• Banking revenue, excluding card processing fees: R$891 million, up 20.0% from a year ago
• Banking gross profit: R$632 million, up 17.9% and now 31.6% of the company total
• Working capital loans: R$820 million, up 170.8% from a year ago and 34.4% from last quarter
• Cash inflows into banking accounts: R$92.2 billion, up 11.1% from a year ago

This expansion matters because banking earns a 70.9% gross margin, compared with 54.0% in payments. Even so, banking gross profit growth has slowed for four straight quarters as the loan book matures and credit provisions rise.

What to watch: fourth-quarter working capital loan originations above the R$299 million third-quarter pace. A higher figure would confirm that small business lending can keep banking revenue growing near 20%.

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
PagBank pays merchants upfront for card sales and collects from card issuers later, so high Brazilian interest rates heavily burden its income statement. Over the past year, those funding expenses held back gross profit.

In the third quarter, financial costs fell 7.2% from a year ago to R$1,294 million. That drop cut financial expenses by 3.1 percentage points of revenue (excluding card processing fees), down to 37.8%. Consequently, gross margin expanded by 1.9 percentage points to 58.4%.

Two forces drove the savings. Brazil's average benchmark interest rate (SELIC) fell 0.94 percentage points from a year ago, and the quarter had one fewer business day. In addition, PagBank funded more of its operations with deposits "predominantly sourced from our own client base, supporting funding cost efficiency and disciplined credit expansion," Mauad said. Interest paid on deposits fell 14.0% to R$972 million, outweighing a 134.2% jump in receivables securitization costs.

What to watch: financial costs as a share of revenue in the fourth quarter. Management's sensitivity table in the financial statements models Brazil's interbank rate (CDI) dipping from 13.65% to 13.15%, which would cut annual net interest expense by R$169 million.

🟢 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞-𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭 𝐄𝐏𝐒
PagBank uses excess capital on its balance sheet to shrink its share count and pay cash dividends. Over the last twelve months, the Brazilian fintech returned R$2.1 billion to investors, including 19 million repurchased shares worth R$1.0 billion.

Those buybacks reduced the diluted share count by 5.6% from a year ago to 278.4 million. Because of the smaller share count, net income growth of 6.9% (excluding one-offs) translated into 13.2% growth in diluted earnings per share, reaching R$2.19. On September 1, the board approved a fourth buyback programme for up to US$150 million, and the firm bought another 1.2 million shares in October.

What to watch: the managerial Basel capital ratio, which ended September at 25.2%. Because that sits well above management's 18% to 22% target range, the group has ample room to execute its new buyback and dividend plan.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐔𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐚𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬
"Portfolio expansion continues to be guided by prudent underwriting standards," Mauad said in the release. To boost lending yields, PagBank is shifting its loan book away from government-backed payroll and severance-fund loans toward higher-risk working capital and credit card loans.

The numbers show that credit risk is rising much faster than the loan book. While the total credit portfolio grew 25.2% from a year ago to R$5.2 billion, unsecured loans more than doubled, jumping 132.0% to R$1.5 billion.

• Unsecured share of total loans: 29.6%, up from 16.0% a year ago and 24.3% last quarter
• Loans 90 or more days past due (NPL 90+): 3.8%, up from 2.6% a year ago and 3.4% last quarter
• Quarterly credit loss allowance expense: R$94 million, up 162.5% from R$36 million a year ago
• Total loan loss reserves on the balance sheet: R$456 million, or 8.8% of the gross loan book

Those higher loan loss provisions reduced banking gross margin by 1.3 percentage points from a year ago to 70.9%. The 6-K filing also shows that past-due working capital loans more than doubled since December to R$276 million, or 33.7% of the gross working capital book by our math.

What to watch: the 90-day non-performing loan ratio and quarterly credit loss provisions in the fourth quarter. If defaults keep climbing faster than interest income as September's working capital cohorts season, credit costs will eat into banking profit.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐌𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥
Processing card payments and advancing cash to merchants against their future card sales still generate nearly three-quarters of PagBank's revenue. Management describes payments as the foundation for cross-selling banking accounts and loans.

That foundation is shrinking. Payments revenue (excluding card processing fees) fell 5.1% from a year ago and 0.9% from last quarter to R$2,533 million. PagBank blamed the drop on product mix and "lower Prepayment to Merchants volumes".

• Prepayment to merchants portfolio: R$44.7 billion, down 1.3% from a year ago and 5.5% from last quarter
• Total payment volume (TPV): R$131.4 billion, up 1.2% from a year ago but down 1.5% from last quarter
• Active merchants: 6.1 million, down 2.2% from 6.3 million a year ago
• Payments gross profit: R$1,369 million, down 1.6% from a year ago and 4.0% from last quarter

Because payments is nearly three times the size of banking, its 5.1% revenue decline wiped out almost all of banking's 20.0% growth. Total revenue excluding card fees rose just 0.4% from a year ago. Moreover, cumulative nine-month gross profit is up only 2.5% from a year ago, well behind the 6% to 9% full-year growth target management set earlier this year.

What to watch: fourth-quarter merchant prepayment balances and payments revenue during the holiday shopping season. Another sequential drop would show that small merchants are permanently using less card prepayment.

🔴 𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡 𝐔𝐩 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝
PagBank kept overall operating costs under control by cutting marketing spend 8.4% and reducing card fraud chargebacks 31.2% from a year ago. However, overhead and legal expenses moved sharply the other way.

Administrative expenses jumped 35.0% from a year ago to R$257 million (or up 31.0% to R$217 million excluding share-based pay and acquisition amortization), adding 1.9 percentage points of revenue by our math. The company attributed this to "higher variable compensation provisions" and a larger share of marketing costs allocated to administration. Meanwhile, net other expenses rose 71.4% to R$76 million on higher labor litigation provisions, lifting total labor contingency reserves on the balance sheet to R$195 million from R$116 million in December.

What to watch: fourth-quarter administrative expenses and labor contingency accruals. If variable pay and legal provisions stay near R$333 million combined, operating leverage will depend entirely on marketing cuts.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐑&𝐃 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐳𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬
A new Brazilian tax law (Complementary Law 224/2025) raised the social contribution tax rate on payment institutions by 3 percentage points in April 2026, pushing PagBank's statutory tax rate from 34% to 37%, with another hike to 15% set for 2028. PagBank fully offset the increase this quarter using R$72 million in technology innovation tax credits (Lei do Bem), R$55 million from lower-taxed foreign entities, and a R$37 million tax claim on loan originations, trimming its effective tax rate to 12.5%.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝐑$𝟒𝟐.𝟖 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Total customer and interbank deposits grew 8.4% from a year ago and held steady against last quarter's R$42.8 billion. Customers on PagBank's own platform supplied 89.8% of those deposits, up from 86.8% a year ago, which allowed the digital bank to trim higher-cost external borrowings by 14.3% to R$3.8 billion.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝐑$𝟒𝟑𝟒.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Spending on payment terminals and software development fell 15.2% from a year ago and 16.1% from last quarter, down to 8.5% of total revenue by our math. PagBank bought fewer card readers (R$164.8 million, down 31.7%) and cut write-offs of inactive terminals by 65.8% to R$13 million, while keeping software investment flat at R$269.8 million.

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝐑$𝟏,𝟕𝟎𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
By our math, operating cash flow of R$2,142 million minus capital expenditures of R$434.6 million produced R$1,707 million in free cash flow, up 2.2% from a year ago and more than triple last quarter's R$491 million. The sequential jump came from a R$1,178 million cash release as merchant card receivables shrank during the quarter.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: ~𝐑$𝟏.𝟑𝟒–𝟏.𝟒𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥. ~𝐑$𝟒𝟎𝟎𝐌 𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐞𝐜 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔)  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from R$1.4 billion
Unchanged. The group has paid R$935 million in dividends through September and approved a fourth payment of US$0.26 per share (about R$400 million) for December 30, 2026, keeping the full-year payout near the R$1.4 billion plan.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔–𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬: 𝐀𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐑$𝟐.𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖  ⇒ stable
New. Mauad stated that PagBank plans to distribute at least R$2.0 billion to shareholders through 2028, alongside the new US$150 million share buyback programme approved in September.

𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐱 (𝐁𝐈𝐒) 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭: 𝟏𝟖.𝟎–𝟐𝟐.𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 18.0–22.0%
Unchanged. "We remain committed to the 18% to 22% target range for our managerial BIS ratio announced in September 2025," the company wrote. The ratio rose 2.7 percentage points from last quarter to 25.2% in Q3, leaving roughly 3 to 7 percentage points of excess capital above the target band.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟔% 𝐭𝐨 𝟗% 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
PagBank did not include its full-year 2026 outlook table in the Q3 release. With nine-month gross profit up just 2.5%, hitting the middle of the 6% to 9% target set earlier this year would require 21.5% fourth-quarter growth by our math.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐭-𝐝𝐮𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟒% 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐤?
Note 9 of the financial statements shows past-due loans (excluding payroll and credit cards) rose from R$125 million in December to R$276 million in September, or 33.7% of the R$820 million gross book by our math. How much of this is early-stage delinquency versus 90-day defaults?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑$𝟑𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦 𝐨𝐧 𝐅𝐆𝐓𝐒 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬?
The tax reconciliation shows 'Other' permanent tax benefits jumped from R$4 million a year ago to R$37 million in Q3, tied to a tax claim on severance-fund (FGTS) loan origination revenue. How much did this trim the effective tax rate, and how long will it recur?

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Prepayment to merchants fell 5.5% from last quarter to R$44.7 billion, pulling payments revenue down 5.1% from a year ago. How much of this drop came from receivables securitization versus lower merchant demand for upfront cash?

Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called WorldParticle, that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture.

Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them.

The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training.  

In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods.

“We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access paper on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.”

Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia.

Unified simulation

For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions.

The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena. 

“If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says.

WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics.

Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. They must convert that complex equation into a formula a numerical solver can handle, repeating these steps for each material and process they want to model.

Instead, the researchers designed a neural network that learns to solve governing equations in general, eliminating the need to design a new model and solver to handle each one. 

Once WorldParticle converts an object into particles, a neural network takes the 3D positions and physical properties of the particles as inputs. It outputs their positions and properties for the next frame of the simulation, predicting the material’s motion over time and space in one-second increments. 

“It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” Chen says.

Before each simulation step, WorldParticle separates the external forces that affect the physical system, like impulse forces that affect an ocean wave when it slams into a seawall. 

After predicting the initial states of the particles, WorldParticle integrates the external forces back into the simulation, correcting its particle predictions based on how those forces affect the object’s behavior. In this way, the system can generalize to unseen materials, changing environmental conditions, and varied forces.

A general, scalable framework

But because a complex object could be broken into millions of particles, the problem quickly becomes too computationally intensive for the model to handle. 

To streamline processing, the researchers employed a merging technique to combine and compress particles while still allowing WorldParticle to capture fine-grained details of their behavior.

“We needed to do a lot of detailed engineering and employ many tweaks to the architecture for it to be truly generalizable and scalable,” Guo says.

They demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials, and proteins, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods. 

For instance, WorldParticle effectively captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. Their method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo adds. 

The general-purpose framework could be applied to many materials and processes, including soft robot manipulation tasks, RNA evolution, and astrophysical phenomena like the merging of galaxies, the researchers say.

Moving forward, they want to adapt WorldParticle to simulate these and other physical systems. They also want to build on this work toward the development of a full, general-purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery. 

 “We see the unification of computation and science giving us new insights and tools to discover physical phenomena or explain some unexplainable physical phenomena,” Guo says. “With a unified model, we could unlock many discoveries that we can’t even imagine.”

Anthropic's updated S-1 adds third-quarter financials and returns the company to a loss. The quarterly numbers sharpen a question the filing already raised: whether revenue can grow fast enough to absorb a compute obligation structure that is largely fixed.

1. Third-quarter revenue was $16.96 billion, up 46.7% sequentially. Compute and infrastructure costs rose 77%, reaching 58% of revenue. The company recorded a $567 million GAAP operating loss. Adjusted operating margin fell from 19% to 15%.

2. Through September, cumulative purchase and lease commitments reached $895.4 billion. About $69.8 billion falls due within twelve months, and roughly half of the total comes due before 2030. Most agreements are take-or-pay, meaning Anthropic owes payment regardless of actual usage.

3. If commitment payments were held to half of revenue, Anthropic would need about $140 billion in revenue over the next twelve months. That is the number implied by the filing, not a forecast. At a 25x multiple, roughly $58 billion in 2026 revenue supports a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion than the original $2 trillion.

4. The pricing pressure is explicit. Anthropic acknowledged in its prospectus that discounts on new model versions and contract concessions partially offset usage-driven revenue gains, with the impact estimated at about $600 million for the quarter. Over 80% of revenue came from models released in the prior six months.

5. Model switching is getting cheaper, and corporate buyers are exercising that option. This is consistent with fintech Ramp's observation that enterprises are rotating between AI providers more frequently. Every reduction in migration cost weakens the pricing power of individual model vendors.

6. Open-weight models are becoming a meaningful supply channel. On OpenRouter and Together AI, token consumption from open-source models is approaching Google Gemini API volumes under comparable measurement. That puts a price cap on closed frontier models rather than leaving them a niche alternative.

7. The harder question sits beyond Anthropic. Model vendors need enterprises to keep increasing compute and API spend. But if the promised productivity gains arrive through labor-cost reduction, they may not create enough new purchasing power to sustain that spend.

Ten @bot templates creators shared on X in the last day: a Costco receipt keeper, a motion-design storyboard library, a landing page critic, a phone-bill advocate, a junk mail stopper, an on-brand image maker, a menopause coach and a rental property scout
Welcome back to the Grok Bot Hall of Fame, the daily roll call of the best @bot templates the community is building.
How inductees are picked: each one was shared on X by its creator between Nov 15 at about 3:15 PM ET and Nov 16 at about 3:15 PM ET, and each post links a template you can import for free. "What it does" comes from the creator's post and the template's own x.ai/bot page. "New drop" means the creator's own post presents it as newly made. Engagement figures were read on Nov 16 at about 3:17 PM ET. This is an editorial pick for usefulness and traction, not a strict popularity chart.
1. Costco Receipt Keeper by @wirelyss · New drop 👑
What it does: Turns your Costco receipts into a private, searchable purchase history you can browse or just ask questions about. Ask about your purchases, find a receipt, and get notified when things you like to buy at Costco go on sale.
Who it's for: Costco members who want to know what they bought, when, and when it's on sale again.
Standout detail: "i just launched Costco Receipt Keeper bot!" The most-liked and most-discussed launch in today's class (66 likes, 27 replies, 12 reposts, about 4.5K views when read).
Why it's in: One store, one job, done well: receipts you can actually search and sale alerts on the things you already buy.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/wirelyss/status
2. Motion Library by @kenn_ronin
What it does: Builds a library of motion design techniques from standout brand and viral videos, learns why they work, and turns them into original storyboards.
Who it's for: Motion designers, video editors and brand teams who want fresh ideas grounded in what already works.
Standout detail: The creator showed a side-by-side of what the AI gave him and what they made after he stepped in: "it had 100 brand motion videos in its head and still needed my taste for 5 rounds." The most-bookmarked post in today's class (80 bookmarks, 51 likes, about 1.6K views when read). The template page credits it as "Motion Library by Tega"; it was shared from @kenn_ronin, who also linked the skill file.
Why it's in: An honest take on AI as extra hands, with a real library behind it.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/kenn_ronin/status
3. Landing Page Copy Critic by @Austen · New drop
What it does: Reads your landing pages the way a first-time buyer does and scores how fast the page says what you do, who it's for, and what to click, then drafts fixes. The creator says it's "loaded with a bunch of skills" to analyze your pages as a first-time viewer and critic.
Who it's for: Founders, marketers and anyone with a page that isn't converting.
Standout detail: Posted as "New Grok Bot." The most-viewed share in today's class (about 5.3K views, 66 bookmarks, 30 likes when read). @Austen is a Hall of Fame returnee.
Why it's in: A first-time-visitor read is the hardest feedback to get on your own page.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/Austen/status
4. Bill by @congressdj
What it does: Your phone-bill advocate for Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and the big prepaid and cable brands. Bill audits your bills and usage and finds cheaper plans.
Who it's for: Anyone who suspects they're overpaying for phone service.
Standout detail: The creator says he's "in the thousands at this point between phone, insurance, fees, etc." and that Bill "started as just a bot to save you a few bucks on AT&T." (His own claim, not verified.) 20 likes and 12 bookmarks when read.
Why it's in: Saving money is the easiest bot pitch there is, and this one has grown beyond its first job.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/congressdj/status

What it does: Turns your phone clips into finished videos with no editing experience needed. It plans the story with you, edits, and checks picture and sound.
Who it's for: People with a camera roll full of clips and no time to learn editing software.
Standout detail: "This is the current version of my video editor. I've compared it to a few others and still prefer this version the best." @MarsHomestead is a Hall of Fame returnee (PhotoFix, Class of Nov 8). 15 likes and 11 bookmarks when read.
Why it's in: A creator's own pick of their best editor build, made for beginners.
Import: x.ai/bot/g-_ahneHRIUAQIyrscdSb
Post: x.com/MarsHomestead/status
6. Junk Mail Stopper by @Kevin_Logan
What it does: Snap a photo of any junk mail that lands in your mailbox and it files that sender's free removal request, then logs every request. It also helps remove you from prescreened credit offers.
Who it's for: Anyone tired of paper junk mail and credit card offers.
Standout detail: One photo is the whole workflow: "Take a picture of the junk mail it does the rest." @Kevin_Logan is a Hall of Fame regular (Bot Sounds, Class of Nov 2; Apple Mac Tools, Class of Nov 6). 14 likes and 8 bookmarks when read.
Why it's in: A real-world chore, handled from your phone camera.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/Kevin_Logan/status
7. Aperture by @AunySillyMe
What it does: An image and short-video maker that asks a few questions about your brand, learns your colors and favorite art styles, then turns a one-line brief into posts, thumbnails, covers and banners.
Who it's for: Creators and small brands who need on-brand visuals fast.
Standout detail: "send a one-line brief, get back a post image, thumbnail or banner in your brand's colors and art style." @AunySillyMe is a Hall of Fame returnee.
Why it's in: It learns your look once, so every image after that matches.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/AunySillyMe/status
8. Menopause Coach by @drbellahqw
What it does: Clear, honest answers about perimenopause and menopause, plus symptom tracking and questions to bring to your appointment.
Who it's for: Women going through perimenopause or menopause, and anyone supporting them.
Standout detail: Built so "you don't walk out wishing you had asked." @drbellahqw is a Hall of Fame returnee.
Why it's in: A health topic that gets too little support, turned into better doctor visits.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/drbellahqw/status

What it does: Scans the official X accounts of crypto exchanges (Binance first, plus Bybit, Bitget and OKX) for events and giveaways, keeps only the ones you can still join, and ranks a Top 5 by effort and cost.
Who it's for: Crypto users who chase exchange promos but hate scrolling for them.
Standout detail: Say "go" for a list on demand, or get it weekly. @toannhu_it is a Hall of Fame returnee.
Why it's in: It filters out expired promos so you only see ones you can still enter.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/toannhu_it/status
10. Rent Scout by @Biggs237
What it does: Finds homes and 2 to 4 unit properties you could buy and rent out, then runs the numbers: rent comps, taxes, cash flow, cap rate and red flags.
Who it's for: First-time and small real estate investors.
Standout detail: Pitched as a way to find properties that "can be rented out to increase your income while paying for the property." @Biggs237 also shared Fed Path, a guide for breaking into federal GS jobs, today.
Why it's in: The math most people skip before buying a rental, done for you.
Import: x.ai/bot
Post: x.com/Biggs237/status

That's the class of Nov 16.
Ten builders, ten free templates. Thanks to @wirelyss, @kenn_ronin, @Austen, @congressdj, @MarsHomestead, @Kevin_Logan, @AunySillyMe, @drbellahqw, @toannhu_it, and @Biggs237 for sharing what they built.

Tencent's new cheap tier may be the Hy4 most agent workloads should actually call: $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output, against $0.834 and $2.501 for full Hy4.

What Tencent launched Nov 16:
• Hy4 flash: 224B total parameters, including 64B of what Tencent calls Engram parameters, with 12B active per token. Natively multimodal, 1M-token context (API limits of 960K in and 64K out)
• Tencent says hybrid attention, LatentMoE and Engram cut the KV cache to 1/24 of Hy3's and 1/6 of Hy4's. For long-context serving cost, that is the line to watch
• Post-trained by self-distillation from Hy4, with RL cutting average end-to-end output tokens by 50%
• Megakernels, 4-bit quantization and DFly push decoding past 150 tokens/s
• On Tencent's own WorkIndex (slides, documents, spreadsheet repair, audio and video), slightly above Hy4 preview at 1/20 of Hy4's cost per task. In a blind test with 85 internal users across 259 tasks, satisfaction landed close to Claude Haiku 5.5
• API id hy4-flash, compatible with OpenAI Chat Completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages. Free in WorkBuddy and 50% off on TokenHub until Nov 30. OpenRouter and open weights are planned

Why it matters for engineers: in high-volume agent steps like search, extraction and doc edits, the bill is driven by output tokens and cache. A model trained to say less, with a much smaller KV cache, attacks both.

The caveats: every number is Tencent's, on its own benchmark and its own users. Tencent still recommends full Hy4 for long-horizon software engineering. And there is no date yet for the weights.
